title: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (adult)
subject: gastroenterology
summary: Classic heartburn or regurgitation without alarm features: 8-week once-daily PPI trial taken 30 to 60 minutes before a meal, then try to stop. Alarm features, non-response or multiple Barrett risk factors need endoscopy (ideally 2 to 4 weeks off PPI). Keep long-term PPI at the lowest effective dose and only with a clear indication.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Classic symptoms: heartburn and regurgitation. Heartburn responds to PPIs more reliably than regurgitation or extra-oesophageal symptoms.
Alarm features needing endoscopy first: dysphagia, weight loss, GI bleeding or anaemia, and persistent vomiting.

Extra-oesophageal presentations (chronic cough, laryngitis, asthma, non-cardiac chest pain): exclude non-GERD causes first; cardiac chest pain must be ruled out before attributing chest pain to reflux.
Barrett's oesophagus risk factors: chronic GERD, male sex, age over 50, White ethnicity, smoking, central obesity, family history of Barrett's or oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

sections.title: Lifestyle
items: Weight loss for patients with overweight or obesity.
Avoid meals within 2 to 3 hours of bedtime.
Elevate the head of the bed for night-time symptoms.
Avoid individual trigger foods only when they clearly provoke symptoms; blanket dietary restriction is not needed.

sections.title: Empiric PPI trial
items: Classic symptoms without alarm features: standard-dose PPI once daily for 8 weeks, taken 30 to 60 minutes before a meal (usually breakfast), not at bedtime.
Good response: attempt to stop the PPI (taper or stop outright; warn about transient rebound symptoms).
Partial response: check adherence and timing, then increase to twice daily or switch to a different PPI once. More than one switch is not supported.

Symptoms that return after stopping: restart at the lowest effective dose; on-demand or intermittent PPI is reasonable for non-erosive disease. If GERD was never objectively confirmed and long-term PPI is planned, confirm it by endoscopy with reflux monitoring off PPI.
H2 receptor antagonists are less effective than PPIs for healing and maintaining erosive oesophagitis; a bedtime dose may help night-time symptoms but tachyphylaxis limits long-term use.

sections.title: Endoscopy and reflux testing
items: Endoscopy first for dysphagia or other alarm features, and for chronic GERD with multiple Barrett risk factors.
No adequate response to the 8-week trial: endoscopy, ideally after stopping PPI for 2 to 4 weeks. If there is no erosive oesophagitis or Barrett's, arrange prolonged (wireless) pH monitoring off PPI.
LA grade C or D oesophagitis: repeat endoscopy after 8 weeks of PPI to confirm healing and look for Barrett's oesophagus.
Isolated extra-oesophageal symptoms without typical heartburn or regurgitation: reflux testing before starting PPI therapy.
Objective evidence of GERD (endoscopy or pH monitoring) is required before baclofen, anti-reflux surgery or endoscopic therapy.

sections.title: Long-term and refractory disease
items: LA grade C or D oesophagitis, peptic stricture and Barrett's oesophagus: maintenance PPI indefinitely (or anti-reflux surgery).
Potassium-competitive acid blockers (vonoprazan) may be used for healing and maintenance of LA grade C or D oesophagitis; they are not advised as first line for grade A or B disease (AGA 2024).
Do not use prokinetics unless gastroparesis is proven, and do not use baclofen without objective evidence of GERD.
Objectively confirmed GERD with persistent regurgitation or preference to stop medicines: refer for laparoscopic fundoplication or magnetic sphincter augmentation by an experienced surgeon.
Obesity with GERD being considered for bariatric surgery: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass is the preferred operation.

sections.title: PPI deprescribing (AGA 2022)
items: Review every long-term PPI regularly and document the indication.
No definite indication: trial of deprescribing. Twice-daily users with a clear indication should usually step down to once daily.

Do not deprescribe in Barrett's oesophagus, severe erosive oesophagitis, oesophageal ulcer or peptic stricture, eosinophilic oesophagitis, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, or high upper GI bleeding risk.
Stop PPIs because the indication has lapsed, not out of fear of reported long-term adverse effects (ACG 2022: high-quality studies show no significant excess risk apart from enteric infections).

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Taking the PPI at bedtime or after food instead of 30 to 60 minutes before a meal.
Endoscopy while on PPI in a patient with an unclear diagnosis: mild oesophagitis heals and the test becomes non-diagnostic.
Labelling cough, hoarseness or chest pain as reflux without excluding other causes.
Continuing lifelong PPI after an 8-week trial without ever attempting to stop.

drugs.name: Omeprazole
drugs.dose: 20 mg orally once daily, 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast, for 8 weeks
drugs.notes: May increase to twice daily for partial response.

drugs.name: Pantoprazole
drugs.dose: 40 mg orally once daily before breakfast for 8 weeks

drugs.name: Esomeprazole
drugs.dose: 20 to 40 mg orally once daily before breakfast
drugs.notes: 40 mg is commonly used for healing erosive oesophagitis.

drugs.name: Rabeprazole
drugs.dose: 20 mg orally once daily before breakfast
drugs.notes: Standard-dose alternative; lansoprazole 30 mg once daily is another.

drugs.name: Vonoprazan
drugs.dose: 20 mg orally once daily for 8 weeks to heal erosive oesophagitis, then 10 mg once daily for maintenance
drugs.notes: Consider for LA grade C or D disease; not first line for milder disease.

drugs.name: Famotidine
drugs.notes: Add-on for night-time symptoms; tachyphylaxis with continuous use. Reduce dose in renal impairment.
